sources.title: Nick Bostrom, Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?
sources.access_level: complete PDF retrieved; relevant full-text passages read

claim_relationships.claim: The argument yields a disjunction: near-zero fraction of human-level civilizations reach posthumanity, near-zero fraction of posthuman civilizations can and will run many ancestor-simulations, or nearly all human-type observers are simulated.
Substrate independence and computational estimates are premises; the simulated-observer fraction is an outcome, not an assumed premise.
The first-person credence step uses a weak indifference principle and assumes no relevant evidence distinguishes simulated from biological observers.

The paper establishes a disjunction, not that the simulation horn is more likely; conditional on that horn credence is high, while the conclusion tentatively suggests roughly even credence across horns under ignorance.

sources.limitations: Bostrom treats substrate independence as an assumption and does not prove consciousness can be simulated; source support does not establish that the argument succeeds.

sources.title: Nick Bostrom, Pascal's Mugging
sources.access_level: complete three-page PDF retrieved and read
sources.locations_reviewed: Pages 443–445; especially p. 444 for utility, probability, and decision assumptions; p. 445 for the ending and footnote on the label.

claim_relationships.claim: Bostrom's Pascal assumes unbounded utility, linear happy-day valuation, no risk aversion or temporal discounting, and assigns nonzero credence to the mugger's finite promises.
The result is conditional on the story's expected-utility assumptions and does not show that any small-probability claim forces acceptance.
Bostrom's footnote credits Yudkowsky with naming the problem.

sources.limitations: The dialogue dramatizes a decision-theory setup; it does not establish a general solution to Pascal's Mugging.

sources.title: Nick Bostrom, The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents
sources.access_level: complete author-hosted PDF retrieved; relevant full-text sections read

claim_relationships.claim: Bostrom defines relevant intelligence as instrumental reasoning and says more or less any level can in principle combine with more or less any final goal, subject to constraints.
Orthogonality and instrumental convergence are separate theses; the latter concerns instrumental values useful for a wide range of goals and situations.
Bostrom discusses moral facts and Humean motivation without making orthogonality depend on Humeanism; final-goal changes differ from routine subgoal changes.
Logical possibility does not make arbitrary or human-respecting goal installation practically easy.

sources.limitations: The paper presents a philosophical thesis and examples; it does not predict the goals of any current AI system.
